newsitem.title: USA: U.S. says progress limited on Japan trade rows.
newsitem.headline: U.S. says progress limited on Japan trade rows.

text.p: The United States and Japan have made enough progress on port access talks to defer U.S. sanctions until September but movement on civil aviation has been much more limited, the State Department said on Monday.

"These are two important trade issues with Japan. ... I cannot report full satisfaction on either of them although more on the ports and less on civil air," department spokesman Nicholas Burns told reporters.

Japan and the United States signed a Memorandum of Consultation on Friday addressing the major issues discussed during 10 days of talks. Maritime Administrator Albert Herberger said Japan agreed to approve applications from U.S. carriers for operations at Japanese ports and to deregulate the licensing system for port transportation business.
On the issue of competition for stevedoring services in Japan, negotiators endorsed an interim agreement providing a framework for reforming the system by July 31, Herberger said.

He gave no details of the plan but Burns said on Monday Japanese government officials would consult with authorities who control Japanese ports "to make sure American firms will then have adequate access to compete for contracts."
"We've essentially kicked the can down the road until Sept. 4, '97" on this issue, Burns said, adding:

"We hope by Sept. 4 to resolve all the (port access) issue so that the Japanese port system will be open to international bidding and that firms like Sea-land Corp. (in North Carolina) will be free to compete on a fair basis with Japanese firms and other firms for the very lucrative port services."

He said the State Department agreed with the Federal Maritime Commission that sanctions should not be imposed as planned on Monday "because of this limited progress that was made." But he said "there has to be progress by Sept. 4" in resolving the remaining differences.

The commission said in February it would impose penalties of $100,000 per visit on Japanese carriers calling at American ports as of April 14 if Tokyo did not move quickly to open access to Japanese ports.

Washington contends its shipping firms are treated unfairly by Tokyo, which maintains tight controls on licensing of stevedores and port operations in Japan. U.S. firms want to be able to hire their own stevedores and set up their own operations, claiming they could save money and improve productivity.

The United States and Japan have also held long-running negotiations on civil aviation, including a round of talks that ended last week. On that subject, Burns said: "I can't point to any progress on those negotiations. We did not resolve the outstanding issues on a fully liberal market-oriented approach to civil aviation, to our proposal for an open-skies regime.

"We hope that the Japanese government will reflect on this and would agree with us in subsequent negotiations that we ought to have freer access to each other's air routes and air ports and air services than curently exist," he said.
